title: The Slow Inventory
premise: Edmund Ashgrove has spent fifteen years writing postcards to her late mother at an address that no longer exists, working as a ghostwriter of other people's letters while living like a guest in her own life. When the crumbling house on Fenwick Lane—where she and her estranged brother Thomas grew up, and where their father's death fractured the family—is scheduled for auction and demolition, Edmund returns to the town she fled. Sorting through the house's slow inventory of objects, letters, and silences with Thomas, she uncovers the truth about the night their father died: that her mother chose to protect Edmund from a blame that was never hers. As the auction date closes in, Edmund must decide whether to bid on a past she can't afford or finally claim a future; the novel ends with the house sold to strangers, but Edmund writing her first postcard addressed to someone still living.
about_author: Rafael Galloway is the pen name of a former estate appraiser who spent a decade cataloguing the belongings of the dead and the departed. The Slow Inventory is his second novel, drawn from the letters he was never asked to send.

chapters.title: Poste Restante
chapters.summary: Edmund, in third-person limited POV, writes her weekly postcard to her dead mother at a burned-down address, then ghosts a wedding toast for a client who barely knows the groom. The beat is quiet loneliness disguised as routine; we learn she hasn't owned anything—a home, a decision—in years.

chapters.title: The Notice
chapters.summary: A certified letter arrives: the Fenwick Lane house enters probate auction in six weeks. Edmund's POV; she recognizes the handwriting on the envelope as her brother Thomas's solicitor. Emotional beat: panic masquerading as indifference, and the first crack in her carefully maintained invisibility.

chapters.title: What the Fire Kept
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter in Edmund's POV: the fire that destroyed her mother's last apartment, and how Edmund let everyone believe she'd been unreachable that night. Beat: guilt established as the engine of her exile, though the reader senses the story isn't what Edmund tells herself.

chapters.title: Return Ticket
chapters.summary: Edmund takes a bus to Marlow Bend, telling no one. Third-person limited. She stands outside the boarded house as a neighbor, Mrs. Okonkwo, greets her by name—the first person in years to do so without transaction. Beat: the unsettling warmth of being remembered.

chapters.title: Thomas, Counting
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Thomas, who has catalogued every room for the auctioneer. He is furious Edmund came, convinced she'll sabotage the sale. Beat: we see his grief is inventory-shaped—he counts because feeling would undo him—and his resentment hides a question he can't ask.

chapters.title: Room by Room
chapters.summary: Edmund insists on helping sort before the sale; Thomas refuses, then relents when she correctly identifies which objects matter. Alternating close-third. Beat: reluctant collaboration, two people negotiating through objects what they cannot say aloud.

chapters.title: The Blue Room
chapters.summary: Edmund finds her childhood bedroom sealed since the funeral. Inside: her mother's unsent letters, dozens of them, addressed to Edmund care of the burned address. POV: Edmund. Beat: vertigo—her ritual of postcards mirrored back at her, revealing her mother wrote too, and never sent.

chapters.title: Auction Fever
chapters.summary: Thomas POV. A developer, Callum Reeve, makes a private pre-auction offer well above reserve. Thomas wants to take it; the money would settle his debts. Beat: temptation and the sense that selling fast means burying something faster.

chapters.title: Letters Not Sent
chapters.summary: Edmund reads her mother's letters chronologically, learning her mother knew about the night their father died—that Edmund wasn't to blame, that someone else was there. POV: Edmund, interleaved with letter excerpts. Beat: hope arriving as dread; the truth has a shape now.

chapters.title: Mrs. Okonkwo's Kitchen
chapters.summary: Edmund confides partially in Mrs. Okonkwo, who reveals the town's version of events differs from Edmund's memory. Third-person limited. Beat: the disorienting discovery that invisibility was never achieved—everyone watched her leave, and everyone waited.

chapters.title: What Thomas Buried
chapters.summary: Thomas POV. He finds Edmund reading the letters and erupts; a fight cracks open the fact that Thomas was in the house the night their father died and has carried a secret of his own. Beat: the siblings' war over the house revealed as a war over testimony.

chapters.title: The Night, Version One
chapters.summary: Edmund reconstructs her memory of her father's death: the argument, the stairs, her running into the storm. Interleaved flashback and present. Beat: memory proves unreliable; Edmund realizes she may have built fifteen years of exile on a misremembered foundation.

chapters.title: Appraisal
chapters.summary: The auctioneer's appraiser walks the house with both siblings present, assigning values. A trivial object—Edmund's father's broken watch—stops the room. POV alternates. Beat: the absurd gulf between market price and meaning; Thomas quietly pockets the watch.

chapters.title: Callum Reeve's Offer
chapters.summary: Reeve courts Edmund directly, offering to let her buy out Thomas's half at a discount if she signs quickly. His charm is genuine and predatory at once. POV: Edmund. Beat: the first real choice—money and erasure, or time and truth.

chapters.title: Version Two
chapters.summary: Thomas, cornered by the letters, finally tells his account: he saw their father fall, and their mother made him swear silence to protect Edmund from a coroner's inquiry into the father's drinking. POV: Thomas. Beat: confession as both wound and relief; the siblings' alliance begins.

chapters.title: The Mother's Last Letter
chapters.summary: Edmund finds the final unsent letter, written days before her mother's death, asking forgiveness for choosing silence over truth. POV: Edmund, alone in the blue room overnight. Beat: grief transfigured—the exile was mutual, and it is over if she lets it be.

chapters.title: Demolition Date
chapters.summary: Reeve accelerates: the auction moves up ten days. Thomas wavers under debt pressure; Edmund offers him the only thing she has—her savings—to delay. POV: Thomas. Beat: sacrifice offered clumsily, refused angrily, then accepted in the novel's quiet turning point.

chapters.title: Open House
chapters.summary: Pre-auction viewing; the town walks through the house. Neighbors leave notes, memories, corrections. Edmund stands in the doorway greeting them. POV: Edmund. Beat: belonging discovered not in ownership but in witness—the community claims the house's story with her.

chapters.title: Bidding
chapters.summary: Climax. At auction, Edmund bids against Reeve with money she doesn't have; Thomas unexpectedly joins, pooling the watch's unexpected value and his own stake. They lose the house—but win something else: Reeve, moved by the crowd's testimony, agrees to preserve the facade and the blue room's contents. Beat: loss reframed as inheritance of a different kind.

chapters.title: Emptying
chapters.summary: The siblings pack the last boxes together, laughing for the first time. Edmund gives Thomas the watch; Thomas gives her the letters. POV alternates. Beat: the inventory complete—not of objects, but of debts forgiven.

chapters.title: Keys
chapters.summary: Edmund rents a small flat above Mrs. Okonkwo's shop and takes a job writing letters for townspeople who can't—for grief, for love, for apology—but this time signs her own name beneath theirs. POV: Edmund. Beat: staying visible as a daily practice, not a single act.

chapters.title: The First Living Address
chapters.summary: Final chapter: Edmund writes a postcard to Thomas, care of the new apartment he's found nearby, and drops it in the box. Last image: the mail truck, the intact facade of Fenwick Lane, spring beginning. Beat: resolution—love chosen over duty's long silence, belonging claimed in the act of reaching out.
